text:
Essays and Classwork
Each essay has been linked with a short description of it’s topic and a general date that it was written. Each of them are research papers generally centering around themes of law, media, politics, and digital worlds.
 AI, Music, and the Evolution of IP Frameworks (In Progress)
This is an essay investigating the legal implications of AI in the Entertainment Industry. I follow the development of Intellectual Property and Entertainment Law, using key cases regarding music sampling to argue for conscientious use of AI, especially in content creation, and highlight emerging blind spots in media regulation. This is actively being written, and has been in progress for a few months. Click the link above to see more from the Claremont Journal of law and Public Policy.
Writing for: Claremont Journal of Law and Public Policy
Started In: Fall 2024
Prejudicial Posthumanism: A Racialized Reframing of Artificial Life Narratives
This essay explores the intersection of posthumanism, AI, and societal biases, particularly in Western culture. It argues that narratives surrounding artificial life, from ancient myths to modern science fiction, reflect and perpetuate deeply ingrained prejudices. As AI develops, these biases may be amplified, shaping how we understand and interact with AI technologies. The essay critically examines how films like Blade Runner and Ex Machina mirror fears of subjugation, servitude, and racial oppression, projecting these anxieties onto AI. It emphasizes the need to reconsider AI narratives to avoid replicating historical injustices, calling for a future where AI promotes ethical coexistence and mutual growth.
Written in: Spring 2024
For: Cinema and AI - Pomona College
^Also published in The Loop
The Internet: A Reframing of the Bridge Between the Real and the Fake
This essay explores how social media bridges digital and physical activism, countering claims that it fosters only passive engagement. It examines the role of weak and strong ties in activism, the free-rider problem in movements, and how decentralized digital organizing mobilizes resources and drives collective action. It also highlights how online activism legitimizes movements and mirrors historical grassroots efforts. Ultimately, the essay reframes social media as a powerful tool for political organizing with real-world impact.
Written in: Fall 2023
For: Political Dialogue and Resistance - Pomona College

title: The Loop
text:
The Loop is a product of the collective work of students across the five Claremont Colleges. Created by Circuits, Internet, Media, and Software, The Loop has published one issue, and the second is currently in progress! Submit here! We don’t discriminate!
As a Co-founder, I am incredibly proud of the momentum, content, and community this magazine and organization has fostered in such a short amount of time, allowing me and my peers to grow as both artists, organizers, and multimedia fanatics. See more about CIMS here.
I independently curated and edited each submission, designed each page, and led print distribution with stringent time constraints. This magazine was primarily meant to be humanitarian, platforming and dignifying student works that would otherwise be forever stuck in their files; however, it has developed into a more mature, formalized production as the organization behind it - CIMS, founded by me and my peers as well – has grown due to my persistent scouting of new E-Board members, student works, and potential events. We host workshops for professional skill building (Raspberry Pi, FL Studio, etc.), opportunities for content creation (various production projects), and community engagement events for club members (powerpoint nights, WingStop mixers, etc.). Each event engages with internet culture and unrecognized digital niches that usually go unseen.
This experience has prepared me to report on, organize, and advise people and ideas, especially those related to media, technology, and culture. Having to collaborate extensively across a wide variety of academic disciplines has allowed me to gain the necessary experience to begin learning the ropes of doing so professionally.

title: Hi-De-Ho: Honoring Cab Calloway, the Rotoscope, and Media History
text:
^^^listen to Icon - Jaden Smith to hear this sampled!
This is an ongoing project, planned to be completed in early April, focusing on a specific clip from a Betty Boop cartoon featuring a rotoscoped animation of a ghost dancing. The original footage, traced over to create the animation, was a performance of “Minnie the Moocher” by Cab Calloway and his Cotton Club Band—an influential group that played a role in laying the conceptual groundwork for MoTown and Black Hollywood’s rise to prominence throughout the 20th century.
While the animated version has become an iconic artifact, even evolving into a meme, it has overshadowed its source material, simultaneously preserving and erasing history. This project will explore how animation can both immortalize and obscure cultural contributions, examining the interplay between adaptation and historical visibility. The final product will be a few-minute-long animated short that traces key moments in animation and music history, incorporating stylistic recreations, backtracking, and archival references.
This project involves a monumental amount of research and attention-to-detail! Did you know that in rotoscoped animation, there are a minimum of 12 frames for every that must be animated? Going into this, I didn’t! My research has centered on both the technological process and cultural progress that has ensued since the Rotoscope’s invention.
The short will feature clipped performances from Cab Calloway, the Nicholas Brothers, Janet Jackson, and other, more contemporary musicians; as well as references to key moments in culture, specifically from the perspective of a young adult who was raised on music videos (me).

text:
about me
My name is Jazzmin, or Jazz, and I am currently a Junior at Pomona College studying Media Studies and Data Science, with a concentration in Electronic Media Production. I’ve bounced around several different interest areas – including (but not limited to) AI, Intellectual Property Law, DJing, and News Writing – which I’ve been enabled to engage with through the technical and creative breadth of Data Science and Media Studies combined.
Data transfers, radio signals, news casts, remixed tracks; it’s all information that’s been diced up to appeal to or be understood by different subjects. This concept, that everything we process (including media) is just re-purposed data, is not new; however, it has underpinned my extracurricular and professional pursuits.
I love to experiment with boundary-stressing avenues of expression through data and culture, particularly through writing, music, and video editing. Chopping and screwing visual, sonic, numerical, textual, and historical data, I aim to broach the worlds of entertainment journalists, marketing professionals, creative directors, and talent managers; bridging my creative ability to craft complex narratives with my passions for arts and entertainment through high-impact, culturally relevant, collaborative projects.


about my work
I have been writing as a journalist for 6 years; producing audio-visual content (documentary film, infographics, fan-edits, music, etc.) for 3 years; and managing several coinciding cross-disciplinary projects for 2 years. From The Knight Times Newspaper to The Post Newspaper of Galveston County to The Feedbacker, I’ve maintained a pointed interest in pop-culture developments and entertainment news, varying between print and visual media as mediums for storytelling through my reporting. Starting Circuits, Internet, Media, + Software (CIMS), my on-campus production organization, has been my boldest step in embracing this vision of a multi-media, interdisciplinary work environment.
Publishing The Loop – a Zine collection dedicated to dignifying and platforming student artwork, writing, software, and interactive media projects – under CIMS, as well as maintaining scheduled community engagement and education events, is one of my proudest achievements, skill- and concept-wise; one that I am looking forward to expanding upon professionally. Bringing fandom communities and underground niches to the forefront of the 5C community through DJ sets, social media campaigns, and production projects, I have developed a knack for developing, following, and platforming marginalized voices through my creations.
Embracing music, film, and writing as chosen mediums, I am looking to pursue a career in entertainment journalism, design, music A&R, or creative content development where I can continue to hold my hand to the pulse of pop-culture, challenge arbitrary boundaries, advocate for underrepresented voices, platform important conversations, and investigate how people and information interact with one another.

title: Project 4 - Data Ethics
text:
A persistent question in the study of Data Science, particularly in recent years, has been how to develop and implement data-driven strategies or technologies in ways that promote social justice rather than impede its progress or perpetuate existing inequalities, while acknowledging that data science involves politically consequential choices rather than neutral technical decisions. Data classification systems often reinforce structural inequalities despite claims of neutrality, which persists from historical to contemporary systems.
Bearing a historical context explicitly based in social science, eugenics, and arbitrary predictive algorithms – systems that classify individuals based on physical traits or their material environment must inform the growing strengths and be informed by the proven weaknesses of predictive classification systems —- regardless of intent or contemporary demands.
We must challenge the notion that data scientists can work as neutral technical actors and begin to recognize them as key political actors engaged in normative constructions of society (privacy, media, space, etc.) to evaluate their work according to its increasing downstream impacts on people’s lives. As Ben Green discusses in “Data Science as Political Action,” establishing a guiding theoretical framework is a crucial next step in understanding the past and potential impacts of scientific conclusions or variance tests.
Green argues that all data science work inherently involves political choices and value judgments about how society should function, even when practitioners don’t recognize this dimension of their work. “ON CRIMINAL ANTHROPOMETRY AND THE IDENTIFICATION OF CRIMINALS,” an experiment conducted by W. R. MacDonnell in 1902 as part of Biometrika, demonstrates an early example of how ignorance towards ethical principles and misplaced partiality can depreciate an experiment’s insights and credibility over time.
Using “Head Length, Head Breadth, Face Breadth, Left Middle Finger, Left Cubit, Left Foot, and Height, of each [observed] individual” to classify and identify potential “criminal classes” and genetic (and environmental) predispositions to crime, this early form of data-driven classification attempted to use statistics and arbitrary measurements to distinguish “habitual criminals” from “non-habitual criminals” and differentiate both groups from the general population, demonstrating an early application of using data to categorize (and police) people.
“Machine Bias” by ProPublica provides a much more contemporary case study of these issues through an investigation of the COMPAS algorithm, which is “used to inform decisions about who can be set free at every stage of the criminal justice system, from assigning bond amounts […] to even more fundamental decisions about defendants’ freedom.” ProPublica found that the algorithm incorrectly labeled Black defendants as higher risk for future crimes at nearly twice the rate of white defendants, despite claiming to be objective and fair.
The data science component across these cases involves collecting, analyzing, and making predictions based on data about people, whether through physical measurements in the early 20th century or complex algorithms (sometimes involving physical characteristics) today. The ethical dilemma emerges when these seemingly objective technical processes reproduce or amplify existing social inequalities and biases, particularly when they impact vulnerable populations through criminal justice systems or social services. The challenge becomes how to develop data science practices that actively work toward justice rather than maintaining a veil of neutrality that often preserves the status quo and echoes the oversights of past conclusions through bias.

title: Project 4 - Data Ethics
text:
Questions

What was the data collection process? Were the observations collected ethically? Are there missing observations?

Reviewing ProPublica’s analysis of COMPAS and W. R. MacDonnell’s findings, a troubling pattern of ethical issues has persisted from early anthropometric criminal identification systems to modern algorithmic risk assessment tools, particularly regarding how data is collected.
In MacDonnell’s hypothesis testing, various physical measurements of a randomly sampled group of 3,000 “non-habitual criminals” were recorded—presumably without informed consent. More specifically, the data was provided to him by a colleague from “the Central Metric Office, New Scotland Yard, where the register of habitual criminals is kept, and their identification effected.” He was given direct access to “a number of ‘practice’ forms which record the metric description of a less pronounced type of criminal than the ‘habituals’—prisoners whose crimes and sentences are comparatively slight, and who may be called ‘non-habitual.’”
Non-habitual criminals were distinguished by the perceived severity of their crime rather than its genuine habituality, which could lead to missing or arbitrary observations. Ethically, these components work together to sour the reliability of the data and resultant findings, as they fail to recognize or mitigate any bias whatsoever; include non-high-society-20th-century-UK-academic perspectives (no diversity in the eyes or hands that touched the data); and consider the ethical implications of each decision made with the data.
The COMPAS risk assessment algorithm investigated by ProPublica similarly raises ethical concerns in the data collection process, as it presumably relies on historical crime data (likely from the individual’s record and past cases that share the same area and potentially the individual’s background) that could reflect decades of discriminatory policing practices and biased arrests. It’s also worth noting that Northpointe, COMPAS’ producer, “does not publicly disclose the calculations used to arrive at defendants’ risk scores, so it is not possible for either defendants or the public to see what might be driving the disparity” between the predicted outcomes of Black and White offenders.
Outside of speculation around the content of the data, Northpointe’s refusal to disclose the variables considered by COMPAS’ algorithm signals a failure to “Prioritize the continuous collection and availability of discussions and metadata.” Through ProPublica’s findings (universally higher risk scores for Black individuals), we can assume that they have also failed to recognize and mitigate bias in the data.
“Data Science as Political Action,” an article by Ben Green—an Assistant Professor of Information and (by courtesy) Public Policy at the University of Michigan—frames these issues theoretically, highlighting how data collection processes claiming objectivity often lack democratic participation from affected communities and fail to acknowledge missing observations from marginalized groups. Across all sources, we see a common theme of data collection that lacks transparency, proper consent, and representation of impacted populations, resulting in systems that reproduce historical patterns of discrimination while claiming scientific neutrality through mathematics, whether using early 20th-century anthropometric measurements or contemporary algorithmic decision-making tools.

What was the permission structure for using the data? Was it followed?

In MacDonnell’s study, no meaningful consent process appears to be documented for those measured and categorized, reflecting an era when ethical standards for research on human subjects were minimal, particularly for prisoners or those deemed “criminal classes.” The contemporary COMPAS algorithm examined by ProPublica represents a modern variant of this issue, where risk assessments are mandatory in many jurisdictions (COMPAS is used in courts in Arizona, Colorado, Delaware, Kentucky, Louisiana, Oklahoma, Virginia, Washington, and Wisconsin), with defendants having no option to opt out despite the profound consequences these assessments have on their lives. Northpointe claims proprietary protection over its algorithm, preventing transparency while collecting sensitive personal data from individuals with little choice.
The “Data Science as Political Action” article once again contextualizes these permission issues theoretically, arguing that the fundamental problem is the lack of democratic consent and participation - data subjects remain objects of analysis rather than participants with agency in how their data is used. All three sources demonstrate a consistent theme of power imbalance in data collection and usage, where those with the least power have their data collected and analyzed with minimal consent, transparency, or recourse.

Who was measured? Are those individuals representative of the people to whom we’d like to generalize / apply the algorithm?

“ON CRIMINAL ANTHROPOMETRY AND THE IDENTIFICATION OF CRIMINALS” explicitly targets individuals already labeled as “criminals,” creating a circular logic where physical measurements are used to identify a “criminal class” based on data from those already in the system, making generalizations inherently biased. Similarly, the COMPAS algorithm investigated by ProPublica is trained on historical criminal justice data reflecting decades of discriminatory policing practices, disproportionately measuring Black defendants while claiming to predict recidivism fairly across populations.
This pattern connects directly to the theoretical framework in “Data Science as Political Action,” which critiques how data science often measures marginalized populations who become subjects of surveillance and control, while those with power remain unmeasured and unscrutinized. The consistent theme across historical and contemporary examples is that measurement tends to focus on already disadvantaged groups, creating systems that claim objective generalizability while actually reproducing and reinforcing existing social hierarchies and biases—the very people subjected to these measurements are rarely representative of the general population, yet the resulting algorithms are applied broadly as though they capture universal patterns of human behavior.

Should race be used as a variable? Is it a proxy for something else?

A central tension across all three references revolves around the use of race (or a proxy for race) as a variable in data systems, revealing how historical prejudices persist in modern algorithms. The 1902 criminal anthropometry study, although not explicitly mentioning race, utilized physical measurements that often served as proxies for racial categorization during an era steeped in eugenics and scientific racism, creating taxonomies of “criminal types” that reinforced racial stereotypes.
The COMPAS algorithm exemplifies the contemporary manifestation of this issue; while it doesn’t directly use race as a variable (to our knowledge), it likely incorporates factors such as criminal history, neighborhood, and family background that serve as proxies for race in a society shaped by systemic inequality, leading to Black defendants being falsely labeled high-risk at nearly twice the rate of white defendants.
Once again providing theoretical context for this pattern, “Data Science as Political Action” argues that seemingly “neutral” variables often encode racial bias, and that treating race as merely a technical variable overlooks how data systems participate in constructing and reproducing racial categories with real social consequences. Across centuries, these cases illustrate how data systems – using both calipers and computers – continue to rely on direct or proxy measurements that entrench racial hierarchies while claiming scientific objectivity.

title: Project 4 - Data Ethics
text:
Conclusion
The evolution of data-driven systems from early 20th-century anthropometric measurements to modern algorithmic risk assessment tools reveals ethical challenges that persist despite superficial fantasies of numerical partiality and bipartisanship.
Despite the increasing sophistication of data science methodologies, fundamental issues remain unresolved: problematic data collection processes that lack meaningful consent; permission structures that disempower those being measured; measurement practices that disproportionately target marginalized populations; and the continued use of race or its proxies in ways that perpetuate historical inequities.
These sources collectively demonstrate that the ethical dilemmas in data science cannot be resolved through technical solutions alone. Professor Ben Green’s framework offers a crucial perspective — that data scientists must recognize themselves as political actors whose work inevitably shapes social outcomes. Whether in the criminal anthropometry of 1902 or the risk assessment algorithms of today, data-driven systems have never been neutral technical tools; they are powerful mechanisms that can either challenge or reinforce existing power structures.
Moving forward requires more than ethical guidelines or algorithmic adjustments; it demands a fundamental reimagining of data science practice that centers justice (for a comprehensive application, a broad redefinition of ‘justice’ is likely needed), incorporates democratic participation from affected communities, and acknowledges the inherently political nature of classifying and predicting human behavior. Without this shift in approach, even the most advanced data science technologies risk perpetuating the same patterns of exclusion and discrimination that have characterized their historical predecessors.

title: Project 2
Project 3
text:
I will conduct a permutation test by simulating behavior under the null hypothesis using the Netflix dataset. This study will explore whether Netflix favors certain genres more than others in its acquisitions. Understanding the patterns in Netflix’s content distribution can provide insights into the platform’s strategic decisions and how they align with viewer preferences and industry trends.
Overview of Process:

I cleaned the data by filtering out missing values, converting dates, and selecting relevant columns
I created a function to calculate the trend in adult-oriented content over time
I used map() to perform a permutation test that shuffles years to determine if the observed trend could happen by chance
I created 3 plots, described below:

Plot 1 - shows the null distribution from the permutation test
Plot 2 - shows the proportion of adult content by year and content type
Plot 3 - shows rating distributions across different time periods


From these tests, we can see different trends over time in the various ratings of content that Netflix provides.




# Loading it in...
netflix <- readr::read_csv('netflix.csv', show_col_types = FALSE)

# Libraries...
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)
library(lubridate)
library(tidyr)

This dataset was originally posted on Kaggle by @paramvir_705, and is updated monthly; it was originally collected from Netflix. The page doesn’t directly indicate further details, so this is assumedly a random chunk of Netflixs’ catalogs, neglecting country lines/firewalls (according to IPVanish, Netflix owns the rights to over 13, 000 titles when accounting for all coutries where they’re active). This is an important caveat to using this dataset, as it will be difficult to draw conclusions about Netflix’s overall behavior.
The dataset contains about 8,800 rows – each a different TV show or movie in Netflix’s catalog – and 12 columns (show_id, type, title, director, cast, country, date_added, release year, rating, duration, listed_in (basically genre)). Testing these variables lets us look for patterns in Netflix’s acquisitions, viewer preferences, and reactions to industry trends.





null (H0): There is no correlation between a show’s rating and its date added to Netflix. As in, the ratings are consistent over time.
alt (H1): There is a correlation between a show’s rating and its date added to Netflix. As in, the ratings get better or worse over time.

netflix <- readr::read_csv('netflix.csv', show_col_types = FALSE)

# Libraries...
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)
library(lubridate)
library(tidyr)

This dataset was originally posted on Kaggle by @paramvir_705, and is updated monthly; it was originally collected from Netflix. The page doesn’t directly indicate further details, so this is assumedly a random chunk of Netflixs’ catalogs, neglecting country lines/firewalls (according to IPVanish, Netflix owns the rights to over 13, 000 titles when accounting for all coutries where they’re active). This is an important caveat to using this dataset, as it will be difficult to draw conclusions about Netflix’s overall behavior.
The dataset contains about 8,800 rows – each a different TV show or movie in Netflix’s catalog – and 12 columns (show_id, type, title, director, cast, country, date_added, release year, rating, duration, listed_in (basically genre)). Testing these variables lets us look for patterns in Netflix’s acquisitions, viewer preferences, and reactions to industry trends.





null (H0): There is no correlation between a show’s rating and its date added to Netflix. As in, the ratings are consistent over time.
alt (H1): There is a correlation between a show’s rating and its date added to Netflix. As in, the ratings get better or worse over time.

title: Project 3
Project 3
text:
map()

set.seed(123)
n_permutations <- 1000

permutation_results <- map_dbl(1:n_permutations, function(i) {
  permuted_data <- netflix_clean |>
    mutate(year_Netflix = sample(year_Netflix))
    rating_trend(permuted_data)
})

p_value <- mean(abs(permutation_results) >= abs(observed_stat), na.rm = TRUE)
p_value

[1] 0.063


This chunk does a permutation test to see the significance of an observed statistic related to Netflix ratings over time. I set a random seed (set.seed(123)) to ensure reproducibility and defined n_permutations = 1000 so that the test will generate 1,000 random shuffles.
In each iteration, the year_Netflix column is randomly shuffled (sample(year_Netflix)) to prevent any connection between time and ratings. I then use the function calculate_rating_trend(permuted_data) on the shuffled data to calculate a new statistic for each permutation; the results are stored in permutation_results.
The p_value (0.063) is calculated as the proportion of permuted statistics that are at least as extreme as the observed statistic (observed_stat), providing a measure of whether the observed trend in ratings is statistically significant. Since 0.063 is slightly above the common significance threshold of 0.05 this suggests that the observed trend (+ 0.06%) is not incredibly statistically significant at the 5% level but is still somewhat insightful. This means there is some evidence of a relationship between year_Netflix and ratings, but it is not strong enough to confidently reject the null hypothesis (which assumes no real trend exists).

title: Project 3
text:
Plot

# Plot 1: Null distribution from permutation test
data.frame(slope = permutation_results) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = slope)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "green", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Null Distribution of Trend Slopes",
    x = "Slope Coefficient",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








This is simply a plot of the null distribution of trend slopes. There is a reletively normal distribution/bell curve, with a few jagged edges; this indicates some variance, with general adhereance to expectations (normal distribution).

# Plot 2: Adult content proportion by year, faceted by type
graphflix <- netflix_clean |>
  mutate(adult_ratings = rating %in% c("TV-MA", "R", "NC-17")) |>
  group_by(year_Netflix, type) |>
  summarize(adult_mean_prop = mean(adult_ratings), n = n()) |>
  filter(n >= 5) 

graphflix |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year_Netflix, y = adult_mean_prop, fill = type)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  facet_wrap(~ type) +
  labs(
    title = "Proportion of Adult-Rated Content on Netflix (TV and Movies) Over Time",
    subtitle = "Adult ratings include TV-MA, R, and NC-17",
    x = "Year Added to Netflix",
    y = "Proportion of Adult Content") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








This graph displays the proportion of adult content in TV Shows and Movies over the years. For movies, we can see that the proportion of adult content added per year isreletively consistent post-2013. Before then, it seems that there was far less adult content, potentially indicating a younger general adience. For TV Shows, there is more variance, especially 2014-2017. There is a dip, potentially indiating a similar change/differnece in audience, or the expiration of deal with a company that produces mature content.

# Plot 3: Rating distribution over time periods, faceted by type
graphflix_2 <- netflix_clean |>
  mutate(time_Period = case_when(
    year_Netflix < 2010 ~ "Early (before 2010)",
    year_Netflix < 2015 ~ "Middle (2010-2015)",
    TRUE ~ "Recent (2018+)"
  )) |>
  group_by(type, time_Period, rating) |>
  summarize(count = n()) |>
  group_by(type, time_Period) |>
  mutate(proportion = count / sum(count)) |>
  filter(proportion >= 0.01) 

graphflix_2 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(rating, -proportion), y = proportion, fill = time_Period)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  facet_wrap(~ type) +
  labs(
    title = "Netflix Content Rating Distribution by Time Period and Type",
    x = "Content Rating",
    y = "Proportion",
    fill = "Time Period"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45))








This graph shows the distribution of proportion of ratings of content over time; that is, each rating is divided into 3 time periods, and the proportion is calculated for each of these periods. This allows us to compare what netflix has attained over time by ratings.
It is clear that before 2010, Netflix likely had a much more mature audience,as they only acquired TV-MA content. They likely diversified their selection as the platform gained popularity in the early 2010s. It is also interesting to see that in TV Shows, Netflix has not aqcuired any PG, PG-13, or R rated content; maybe because of a lack of a demand for television content in these ratings? I think this will likely change soon, given the increasing popularity of knarly and graphic young adult television (see Euphoria) and increasing competition from companies like HBO.

Conclusion
Through this simulation study, I examined whether Netflix’s acquisition patterns reflect a significant trend in the proportion of adult-rated content over time. Using a permutation test, I compared the observed trend to a null distribution of randomly shuffled data, finding a slight increase in adult-rated content per year (~0.6%). With a p-value of 0.063, this trend slightly exceeds the conventional 0.05 significance threshold, suggesting that there may still be a weak trend, but not strong enough to confidently reject the null hypothesis.
The visualization of adult content proportions over time highlights interesting temporal trends, such as a relatively stable proportion of adult-rated movies post-2013 and notable fluctuations in TV shows between 2014-2017. These shifts may reflect changes in audience demographics, licensing agreements, or strategic content investments by Netflix. Additionally, the content rating distributions across different time periods suggest an evolution in Netflix’s offerings, catering to a heavily mature audience pre-2010 and attaining a more diverse content catalog in subsequent years.
Overall, while this study provides insight into Netflix’s content acquisition trends, limitations in dataset representativeness must be acknowledged. Additionally, applying more sophisticated statistical models, such as time series forecasting or causal inference techniques, could further clarify the extent and drivers of observed rating trends.

title: Halloweekend in Claremont - A Documentarian Analysis of 5C Party Promo Culture
text:
This is an amateur documentary that was produced as a group project for my Anthropology of Digital Cultures class. Beginning development in October 2024, 2 of my classmates and I conducted ethnographic research centering the cresting racial, administrative, and political tensions, both internal and external to Pomona College, and their effects on how on-campus parties are promoted, and, more importantly, how the promoters and attendees interact (or don’t) with one another.
This short documentary gives a brief, intimate peek into the parties thrown throughout Halloweekend 2024 (Oct 31 - Nov 2). Examining music, design, communication pipelines, and administrative changes at Pomona since the 90’s, we designed this project to include the documentary below and a complementary ethnographic research paper.

  
    
      
      Your browser does not support the video tag.
    
  

I edited this in it’s entirety using iMovie, designed our interview questions, and filmed about a third of the content; the aesthetics are intentionally unfocused, shaky, and unclear to emulate the chaos and instability reflected both in a night out and emerging political tensions in Claremont at the time. The low quality, however, is for file processing reasons to display on this site (apologies for the 480p!).

title: Cowboy Poker
text:
This shoot was an amateur attempt at an improvised Cowboy-Themed World Series Poker Match. With each player designing their own character, we assumed our chosen roles as we played Hold ’Em for 9 hours to get the appropriate shots, queues, and to finish the game, most importantly.
I played my OC, Psychic Cowboy, who had a pet bear (that they could telepathically communicate with) and who also happened to come into an $80 fortune at the end of the game after a blisteringly tense 3-hour-long stand-off between Psychic Cowboy and another player.
